blocks.text: Based in the Marais in Paris since 2009, the Galerie Jean-François Cazeau builds bridges between the Modern Masters and postwar art on both sides of the Atlantic, while also opening itself to contemporary art. For its first participation in Paris Photo, from November 12 to 15, 2026, at the Grand Palais, and in view of the Bicentenaire de la Photographie (2026–2027), the gallery which has received the French Ministry of Culture’s label for this anniversary event will present a retrospective exhibition devoted to the humanist and Surrealist photographer Pierre Jahan (1909–2003). A selection of some forty photographs, illustrating the different techniques the artist used as well as his various experiments, will allow visitors to rediscover the many facets of his work.

Born in 1909, Pierre Jahan belongs to a generation of photographic pioneers who regard the medium no longer as a scientific or technical practice, but as an art of pleasure and freedom. In this way he joins Henri Cartier-Bresson, Man Ray, Lee Miller, László Moholy-Nagy, Dora Maar and their colleagues across the Atlantic, such as Alfred Stieglitz, in the quest to have photography recognized as an art in its own right, endowed with its own artistic and expressive possibilities. Pierre Jahan is a protean figure of the avant-garde, impossible to classify, who considered photography as a testing ground, the only law being the pleasure of the eye and the hand. Although he never claimed any dogma, always preferring to keep his freedom, fantasy nevertheless remained the common thread running through his work. He married the drive of life with its springs of creation and did not hesitate to experiment with new techniques such as the rayograph, the photogram, double exposure, photomontage and photocollage.

Settling permanently in Paris in 1933, Pierre Jahan joined photographers such as Brassaï, Robert Doisneau and Henri Cartier-Bresson, who were eager to show a different Paris, in all its facets. He moved from images rooted in the real world, at times merciless, such as his pictures of the Occupation or of the fight for the Liberation of Paris, to his imaginary fantasies, at times full of humor. Pierre Jahan has the rare talent of slipping seamlessly between the disparate worlds of reportage photography and Surrealism, particularly at a time when artistic ideologies were unfolding militantly in successive manifestos. Jahan’s work crosses the twentieth century at a slant, unconstrained. It is at times grave and metaphorical, at times wandering and playful, always full of lyricism. The artist practices, and pushes to their limits, all the photographic techniques offered by his time a true testing ground – to create a body of work at once rooted in Surrealism and resolutely singular.
